newsitem.title: LATVIA: LIEPAJA METAL IN 137,400 LATS Q1 PROFIT.
newsitem.headline: LIEPAJA METAL IN 137,400 LATS Q1 PROFIT.

text.p: Liepaja Metalurgs, the only metal producer in Latvia, on Wednesday said that its first quarter profit came to 137,400 lats on net turnover of 6.1 million lats.
Metalurgs also said that the plant plans a 1997 turnover of 32.8 million lats.
"Our production volume has doubled compared to the first quarter of 1996 and all indicators are positive," Valerii Terentjev, the plant's manager, told Reuters.
The company posted a 1996 loss of 1.5 million lats.
Liepaja has more than doubled its rolled metal production to 102,000 tonnes in the first three months of 1997 against 40,000 tonnes in the same period last year.
Steel wire production rose to 3,274 tonnes in the first quarter against 924 tonnes in the same period in 1996.
The volume of nail production was also up, rising to 1,111 tonnes versus 423 tonnes in the first three months of last year, Terentjev said.
The number of employees in the Liepaja Metalurgs has risen to 2,450 against the ceiling of 2,216, set in the privatisation agreement.
Liepaja has its 72 percent controlling stake held by Agrosin Pte, a Russian-Belarussian-Singaporean joint venture, which plans to invest $5.5 million in the company this year.
The sell-off rules demand a three million lats investment to be made in two years time.
The company said that its earlier raw material and gas supply problems have been resolved.
Liepaja, the biggest client of Latvian Gas, had earlier amassed debts which are currently being settled, Terentjev said.
"We have signed an agreement with Latvian Gas on a debt repayment shedule and Agrosin has already made two payments in accordance with it," he said.
He declined to comment on the details of the agreement or the sum of the outstanding debt.
Liepaja plans to use slightly more than 100 million cubic metres of gas this year, close to its annual average.
Liepaja Metalurgs exports its produce to South East Asia, North Africa and the U.S..
"We have not been exporting to the CIS countries for more than five years now," Terentjev said. "Not that there is a lack of demand, but the purchasing power is not there."
